title: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The difficulty in finding extraterrestrial intelligence is not finding systems that compute in sophisticated ways, which are common, but finding ones whose details are similar enough to humans that we would recognize them as intelligent; somewhat generalized intelligence is likely to exist but to behave in bizarrely unhuman ways.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: that the basic issue is not finding systems that perform sophisticated enough computations, but rather finding ones whose details happen to be similar enough to us as humans that we recognize what they do as showing intelligence.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Intelligence in the Universe” (from p. 822), p. 839. Scope: extraterrestrial intelligence

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-52: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.15

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Unlike a purely definitional claim, this proposes how humans would recognize real extraterrestrial agents, so it is testable in principle. No existing dataset contains the required cases, and simulations or fictional agents cannot resolve the intended extraterrestrial scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Given authenticated extraterrestrial agents, measure human recognition judgments and behavioral similarity independently of computational capability. Recognition tracking similarity rather than capability would support the claim; reliable recognition of radically dissimilar agents would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Intelligence and human similarity lack independent ground truth.

No authenticated extraterrestrial intelligence data exist.

The prediction about generalized intelligence is vague.

data existence: 0.15

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a conclusion about what would count as recognizing intelligence, rather than a forecast with a separate measurement. Generalized intelligence that behaves in unhuman ways is, by the sentence's own standard, something we would not count as intelligence. No astronomical or biological dataset distinguishes that stance from rivals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The sentence says the task is to find systems whose details are close enough to humans that we call them intelligent. A system we do not recognize is then either not intelligent or not similar, and the claim does not separate those readings.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Likely to exist is not tied to an observation.

Recognition of intelligence is defined by similarity to humans, so a dissimilar intelligence falls outside the criterion.
